catalog_quote: The Tokyo dialect of Japanese exhibits lexical contrasts based on pitch accent; that is, there are minimal pairs of words that are identical segment-wise, but can be distinguished in terms of their pitch contours ... Japanese makes lexical contrasts in terms of pitch accent in two ways: (i) presence vs. absence, and (ii) if present, location. ... a. ame+ga (unaccented) 'candy+NOM' b. a'me+ga (accented) 'rain+NOM' ... Phonetically speaking, an accented vowel is assigned a High tone followed by a Low tone on the following vowel, resulting in an abrupt H(igh)-L(ow) fall in F0, whereas unaccented words do not show such a fall. ... for words consisting of n-syllables, there are n+1 accent patterns ... a. i'noti+ga (initial accent) 'life+NOM' b. koko'ro+ga (penultimate accent) 'heart+NOM' c. atama'+ga (final accent) 'head+NOM' d. miyako+ga (unaccented) 'city+NOM' ... Japanese allows only one …
sweep_summary: Japanese (nucl1643) is in the catalog as 'tonal' (lexical pitch accent) on Kawahara 2015 (held). Of 66 works with stress in the title, about 30 concern word accent of Tokyo/standard Japanese; the rest are phrasal prosody, other dialects (Kyoto, Kagoshima, Tsuruoka, Koshikijima), proto-Japanese reconstruction, or noise (L2 English accents, rakugo rhythm, palatal 'prosody'). Newly downloaded and read (all with record): McCawley 1965 MIT thesis (open on MIT DSpace), Shimabukuro 2002 UH dissertation (ScholarSpace), Poppe 2015 UTokyo dissertation, Kubozono 2006 Lingua (Kobe repository accepted MS), Ding 2006 (JUL open access), Kibe 2010 (NINJAL repository, Japanese), Ito & Mester 2007/2013/2019 (author copies), Seo et al. 2019 (ICPhS), plus an extra open find not in the list, Weitzman 1970 (USC/ONR instrumental study, ERIC). Every one describes Tokyo Japanese as a pitch accent system: at most one HL fall per word/phrase, lexically present-or-absent and lexically located (n+1 patterns), antepenultimate default in loanwords, F0 not intensity the correlate, no word stress. None contradicts or refines the classification beyond what the held Kawahara 2015 already states; the McCawley 1965 statement is the best new first-hand corroboration but does not supersede Kawahara 2015. Unread items that would deepen but not change the record: Kubozono 2011 (Blackwell), 2012 (Lingua), 2008 (Oxford Handbook) - all paywalled, medium priority; the remaining paywalled/print items (Haraguchi 1988, Nishiyama 2010, Oshima 2014, compound-accent papers, Yoshida 1995 thesis, Bostrom 1993, Kubozono 1993, Akinaga 1985) are low. discovery relied on Crossref, CiNii, Semantic Scholar, DSpace/WEKO APIs and archive.org (OpenAlex and Bing were unusable).

new_statements.quote: A sentence of standard Japanese is divided into phonological phrases (bunsetsu) each of which may contain at most one significant fall in pitch. I will refer to the syllable or mora where this fall in pitch occurs as the accented mora or syllable of the phrase. Then, disregarding intonational factors, the morae of a phonological phrase display the following pitches: the morae up to and including the accented mora are high-pitched, except that the first mora is low-pitched if it is not accented; the morae after the accented mora are low-pitched; in phonological phrases which contain no accented mora, the first mora is low-pitched and all subsequent morae high-pitched.
new_statements.translation: (English original.) Same section continues: 'Japanese differs from languages with "stress accents" such as English and German in that, at least within the word, there is no such thing as secondary stress in Japanese.' Abstract: Japanese's 'accentual system is one of "pitch accent", in which a phrase can be characterized accentually simply in terms of the location of a fall in pitch and in which there is nothing comparable to the several degrees of stress which can be found in a word in English.'
new_statements.citation: McCawley, James D. 1965. The accentual system of standard Japanese. PhD thesis, MIT (Department of Modern Languages), 223 pp. Open copy: MIT DSpace handle 1721.1/13012.
new_statements.locator: Chapter III 'Accent', §3.1 General remarks, p.139 (scanned text lines 4861-4899); abstract p.2
new_statements.reading: Standard (Tokyo) Japanese has lexical pitch accent: at most one HL fall per phrase, its location lexically specified (free, values 1.n syllables, p.56) or absent; H spreads back to the second mora with the first mora low; no word stress and no stress gradations. This is the classic first-hand generative description and fully corroborates the catalog's 'tonal' (pitch accent) coding.

new_statements.relation_note: A speech-perception paper on vowel-length boundaries; subjects are Tokyo-area students. It never describes the accent system, but it treats Japanese word accent as a pitch pattern (H on one mora, L on the next) that varies lexically, which is consistent with the catalog's pitch accent (tonal) coding and with McCawley 1965. Not usable as a primary source for placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Only an incidental presupposition, not a description of the system: Japanese words carry lexical 'accent patterns' realised as pitch (high on one mora, low on the next), and the HL pattern with a high-pitched first syllable and low second is a common pattern across Sino-Japanese and Foreign vocabulary strata. No statement about where accent falls in general.
new_statements.identity_note: Moreton & Amano 1999 used Tokyo-area speakers/listeners (standard Japanese); the silent syntax works (Yatabe, Konno, Fujita, Farmer) concern standard Japanese. The catalog record and McCawley 1965 statement concern standard (Tokyo) Japanese; no work opened here describes another dialect.

new_statements.quote: In sum, the tone pattern of a Tokyo dialect word is described by two parameters: the presence or absence of an initial low mora, and the presence or absence of a fall from high to low. Moreover, the presence of the initial low mora is predictable. The initial mora is high if the first syllable is heavy or if the following mora is low; otherwise, the initial mora is low. The distinctive property of words is, then, the presence and location of the fall from high to low. [p.29] ... Japanese is not usually described as exhibiting any sort of stress independent of the pitch accent system. There is nonetheless some reason to believe that Tokyo dialect Japanese has a stress system of sorts. [p.42]
new_statements.citation: Poser, William John (1985). The phonetics and phonology of tone and intonation in Japanese. Massachusetts Inst. of Technology.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement/type as the existing McCawley 1965 statement (lexically located HL fall, mora TBU, Tokyo dialect); adds the syllable as accent domain and the tentative durational bimoraic rhythm / initial-prominence discussion, flagged as unconfirmed. The MPG PuRe file is audience-restricted; the record's public external link (MIT DSpace hdl 1721.1/15169) was used.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tokyo Japanese has lexical pitch accent: the only distinctive word property is whether and where a high-to-low fall occurs; the initial low mora is predictable (first mora low unless the first syllable is heavy or the second mora is low). The tone-bearing unit is the mora but the accent domain is the syllable (in a heavy syllable the fall can only follow its first mora, p.35). No stress independent of pitch accent is normally recognised.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §1.5 (pp.42-49) discusses a possible non-contrastive 'stress system of sorts': a subjective impression of initial prominence on words (Hattori and Poser's consultants), phrase-final lengthening, and an alternating rhythm of bimoraic feet built left to right with the first mora of each foot stronger, whose 'principal if not only phonetic exponent is found in duration, not F0 or vowel quality' (p.43); Poser states no instrumental investigation had been made.
new_statements.exceptions: Words may be unaccented (no fall). Poser explicitly argues (p.42) that Hattori's prosodeme does not attribute non-tonal correlates to the accent itself.
new_statements.identity_note: Poser describes the Tokyo dialect (standard Japanese), as does the existing McCawley 1965 statement; Fon's Japanese subjects were Tokyo Japanese speakers from Tokyo and three neighbouring prefectures. No other variety is described in the opened works.

new_statements.quote: Japanese is not usually described as exhibiting any sort of stress independent of the pitch accent system. There is nonetheless some reason to believe that Tokyo dialect Japanese has a stress system of sorts. I have already cited Hattori's report that he has the impression of initial stress on words, and other speakers whom I have consulted confirm this subjective impression. Unfortunately, no instrumental investigation of this point has been carried out. In a similar vein, there is some evidence for phrase-final lengthening in Japanese. This suggests that there may be a word-level pattern of increased duration at the end and "stress" at the beginning.

new_statements.quote: Theoretically, a lexical accent may land on any one of the vowels in a word. However, in Standard Japanese, if a word consists of three 'syllables (in traditional terms)' or less, the lexical accent location is random, unlike longer words whose accent location is predictable (Haraguchi 1991). Also, it is said that there is class of nouns without lexical accent. [...] Note that the pitch pattern is predictable if the location of the accent is known. [...] accent location in certain classes of words is predictable, and accordingly Standard Japanese should be regarded as any other stress system: to wit, the stress (accent) location is predictable, if it is not specified lexically.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (lexical pitch accent in Tokyo/Standard Japanese: presence vs absence and location of one accent, pitch contour predictable from it), so no contradiction; adds placement detail not in the Kawahara record or the McCawley/Poser statements: accent location is lexically free only in short nouns (<=3 OR pairs/moras: n+1 classes incl. unaccented), long morphologically simplex nouns and loanwords take default antepenultimate accent, short lexically unmarked nouns surface accentless, the domain-initial nucleus is never high unless itself accented, and compound/verb/phrase accent is derived by the same principles; Yoshida treats the system formally as a stress system.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Standard (Tokyo) Japanese is a lexical pitch accent language: a word has at most one accent (or none); from the accented nucleus leftwards all nuclei except the word-initial one are high, nothing after it is high, so the contour follows from the accent location. In nouns of up to three moras (OR pairs) the accent location (or its absence) is lexical (n+1 classes: na'mida, tama'go, takara', kuruma); morphologically simplex nouns of four or more OR pairs and long loanwords get default antepenultimate accent (mura'saki, hototo'gisu, suto'resu, puro'guramu), analysed as the head of the penultimate right-headed foot; short lexically unmarked nouns surface accentless; compound, noun+particle, verb and sentence accent are derived from the members' lexical properties by the same licensing principles. The author argues the formalism is identical to stress assignment (predictable unless lexically specified).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None posited: only one head (accent) per domain; footnote 6 p.78 says only primary prominence is discussed. No stress independent of pitch accent is claimed anywhere in the thesis.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked short nouns and some loans keep accent off the default site; final-accented and accentless nouns are homophonous in isolation and distinguished only before particles (-ga); 'devoiced' high vowels and the moraic nasal cannot bear accent, shifting it (sec. 3.3); genitive -no deaccents certain final-accented nouns (sec. 4.3.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Yoshida 1995 treats Standard (Tokyo) Japanese; Bostrom 1993 (title) treats Japanese pitch accent generally, presumably Tokyo standard; Otaka 2009 treats standard Japanese rhythm/timing (moras, feet, geminates); Hirata 2006 is Japanese syntax.

tone_statements.citation: Urasoko, Rie. 2023. De-Accentuation in Tokyo Japanese. Radical: A Journal of Phonology, 168-202.
tone_statements.quote: The prominence of a pitch accent is determined by the difference in pitch height. The distinctive lexical pitch accent is marked phonetically by the sequence from high pitched mora (henceforth H) to low pitched mora (henceforth L). This accent is located on the last H pitched mora immediately before the tonal dropping towards L pitched mora, which is called “accent kernel”. Thus, only the tonal fall (HL) marks a placement of lexical accent (if there is one). ... The Japanese lexicon is divided into two accentual patterns: accented and unaccented. ... The accent kernel can be located on any mora.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 169-170, sec. 1.1 'Accent in Tokyo Japanese' (footnote number 1 after 'accent kernel' elided)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo-type pitch accent: words accented (one HL fall, kernel on any mora) or unaccented; H/L are mora pitch heights, no tone count; at least 22 accent-marked forms pp. 170-172.

tone_statements.citation: Urasoko, Rie. 2023. Le patron atone et le phénomène de la désaccentuation en japonais moderne [The atonic pattern and the deaccentuation phenomenon in contemporary Japanese]. Thèse de doctorat, Université Bordeaux Montaigne (dir. Laurence Labrune). NNT 2023BOR30057.
tone_statements.quote: Le japonais est communément catégorisé comme une langue à accent de hauteur ... L’accent lexical du japonais se révèle donc dans la différence de niveau de hauteur mélodique. Il existe en principe deux hauteurs distinctives, haut (désormais H) et bas (B) et le noyau accentuel se situe immédiatement devant la descente tonale. ... contrairement à l’analyse de Poser (1984), ainsi qu’à notre propre analyse basée sur un système à ton H privatif dans lequel B est phonologiquement inactif. ... Nous considérons ainsi, pour notre part, que les éléments que nous avons mis au jour pointent fortement en faveur d’une analyse tonale, au sens plein, du japonais de Tōkyō.
tone_statements.translation: Japanese is commonly categorised as a pitch-accent language ... The lexical accent of Japanese thus shows itself in the difference of melodic pitch level. There are in principle two distinctive pitches, high (henceforth H) and low (B), and the accent kernel is located immediately before the tonal fall. ... contrary to Poser's (1984) analysis, as well as to our own analysis based on a privative H-tone system in which B (low) is phonologically inactive. ... We thus consider, for our part, that the elements we have brought to light point strongly in favour of a tonal analysis, in the full sense, of Tokyo Japanese.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 74-75, §2.3 sub-section 'Accent lexical de hauteur du japonais: noyau accentuel et niveaux de hauteur'; then p. 520 and p. 523, §7.3 'Le japonais de Tōkyō est-il une langue à tons ?'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo Japanese described as pitch accent (H/B, accent kernel before the fall, tonic vs atonic words, mora as accent unit), then reanalysed as privative H-vs-zero tone with floating H, surface H/M/B.

tone_statements.citation: Ito, Junko & Mester, Armin (2019). Pitch accent and tonal alignment in Kagoshima Japanese. The Linguistic Review 36: 1-24.
tone_statements.quote: ...the dialects of Kagoshima Japanese have only two patterns, regardless of the length of the word (“N-pattern systems”). The first is the HL pattern (also called “Type A”), which aligns a H(igh) L(ow) sequence with the end of the word, preceded by a sequence of L-toned syllables. The second is the H pattern (also called “Type B”) which consists in a final H tone, also preceded by L-toned syllables. ... For our purposes here, we follow the tonal analysis of Kubozono (2012) and simply take the two tonal melodies as lexically given.
tone_statements.locator: p. 3, sec. 1 Introduction
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Two-pattern (N-pattern) pitch accent: lexical melodies HL (Type A) vs H (Type B) aligned to the word end, syllable by syllable in Kagoshima City; data from Kubozono.

tone_statements.citation: Kubozono, Haruo. 2017. Accent in Japanese phonology. In Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics. New York: Oxford University Press.
tone_statements.quote: Japanese dialects have pitch accent systems, systems where pitch, rather than intensity or other phonetic features, is used as the primary phonetic property of words (Beckman, 1986 ). Moreover, most dialects, including Tokyo Japanese, use pitch contrastively ... Most of them are sensitive to an abrupt pitch fall and use it as the primary phonetic correlate of the phonological pitch accent (Hattori, 1960 ; McCawley, 1968 ; Pierrehumbert & Beckman, 1988 ). This can be demonstrated by the following data from Tokyo Japanese, where lexical meanings can be differentiated by the presence or absence of a pitch fall as well as the position of the pitch fall.
tone_statements.locator: Section 1.1 'Pitch Accent System', first paragraph
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo Japanese lexical pitch accent: words accented (place of an abrupt pitch fall) or unaccented; (n+1) patterns for n-syllable nouns; no H/L tone inventory; downstep named as a phrasal process.

tone_statements.citation: Ito, Junko & Mester, Armin. 2016. Unaccentedness in Japanese. Linguistic Inquiry 47(3): 471-526. doi:10.1162/ling_a_00219
tone_statements.quote: The phonetic characteristics of Japanese pitch contours ... include two main features, the initial rise and the accentual fall. The pitch contour of a prosodic word—more precisely, of a minor phrase ...—begins with a boundary %Low and then proceeds on a phrasal High until it reaches the accented syllable, if present. The accentual High*Low complex is a steep fall, as on the syllable ra in a form like tabesaseráreta ‘was made to eat’. In the absence of an accent, as in iresaserareta ‘was made to insert’, the pitch stays on the phrasal High. The concatenation of these tones results in the overall pattern %Low+High+(High*Low)%.
tone_statements.locator: p. 474, sec. 2.1 Preliminaries
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo Japanese lexical pitch accent: the accented syllable carries a High*Low fall, docked on its head mora (p. 489, fn. 14); unaccented words stay on phrasal High.

tone_statements.citation: Labrune, Laurence. 2013. Le japonais. Lalies (Langues et littérature: actes des sessions de linguistique et de littérature) 33: 171-219.
tone_statements.quote: Le japonais de Tokyo est connu pour son accent de hauteur ... Les mots japonais appartiennent à la classe accentuée ou inaccentuée. Les mots accentués possèdent une more qui constitue le noyau accentuel du mot, après laquelle se produit une chute tonale. C'est donc le passage d'une tonalité haute à une tonalité basse qui marque la position de l'accent au niveau du mot. Les mots inaccentués ne possèdent pas de passage de haut à bas. ... a) il n'y a qu'un seul passage de haut à bas dans un mot accentué ... b) les deux mores initiales du mot doivent être de tonalité différente, soit haut - bas, soit bas – haut.
tone_statements.translation: Tokyo Japanese is known for its pitch accent ... Japanese words belong to the accented or the unaccented class. Accented words have a mora that constitutes the accent nucleus of the word, after which a tonal fall occurs. It is thus the transition from a high pitch to a low pitch that marks the position of the accent at word level. Unaccented words have no high-to-low transition. ... a) there is only one high-to-low transition in an accented word ... b) the first two morae of the word must differ in pitch, either high-low or low-high.
tone_statements.locator: section 2.5 L'accent (no page numbers; published version pp. 171-219)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo pitch accent: accented vs unaccented words; accent-nucleus mora followed by an HL fall; surface H/B patterns from two principles; minimal pairs (hashi); accent mainly demarcative/culminative.

tone_statements.quote: At the level of general description, however, most Japanese linguists and generative phonologists agree on several basic points: (1.1) a. tone_statements.quote: (4) Pitch Accent Principle A pitch accent language has only one pitch, high pitch, which is the immediate interpretation of a pitch accent. ... A (lexical) accent is interpreted as a high pitch, thus an accented vowel is high-pitched. ... In the same manner, in Standard Japanese, the accented nucleus is high-pitched and the other nuclei are simply not high-pitched, that is, pitchless. ... Vowels which are not high-pitched have been said to bear a low tone (Haraguchi 1977, 1991, Poser 1986, Matsumori 1989). There is, however, no evidence for the existence of another tone/pitch. To call what is not H-toned "low-toned" is unwarranted: such vowels are merely pitchless

tone_statements.quote: (12) 1. The primary phonetic feature of the accent is a sudden drop in pitch. 2. tone_statements.quote: As shown in (1), verbs in Japanese fall into two prosodic classes: those with accent and those without. Accent on verbs in the accented class typically falls on the penultimate mora or vowel. A small subset of verbs, however, always exhibit accent on the antepenultimate mora, as in (2). By analogy with the shift of accent leftward away from devoiced high vowels (McCawley 1965; Varden 1998), we refer to this antepenultimate accent pattern as accent shift. As (2) illustrates, all accent shift verbs are of the shape ...VV(C)V; they have no consonant between the antepenultimate and penultimate vowels, placing those vowels into hiatus. However, only ten of these "shift-eligible" verbs always exhibit accent shift.

tone_statements.quote: The dialects of Japanese are divided into three main groups, the Tokyo-type dialects, the Kansai-type dialects, and the accentless dialects. The differences between these three groups are primarily in their pitch accent systems, not in the segmental phonology. [...] For the Tokyo-type dialects, the only aspect of the pitch accent system which is distinctive is the place of pitch fall within a word. Pitch falls after the accented mora, and the first mora of a word is predictably low unless the word has initial accent, so in a word with an accent somewhere other than the first mora, the first mora is low, all moras from the second to the accented one are high, and all moras after the accented one are low. Words with no accent remain high through the last mora. [...] The Kansai-type dialects have this same distinction, but in addition, they distinguish between high-beginning and low-beginning words (examples in 2). The Kansai dialects also have surface final contour tones (rising or falling, abbreviated A for ascending and D for descending) which the Tokyo-type dialects lack.

I will refer to the syllable or mora where this fall in pitch occurs as the accented mora or syllable of the phrase. Then, disregarding intonational factors, the morae of a phonological phrase display the following pitches: the morae up to and including the accented mora are high-pitched, except that the first mora is low-pitched if it is not accented; the morae after the accented mora are low-pitched; in phonological phrases which contain no accented mora, the first mora is low-pitched and all subsequent morae high-pitched. [...] It will be noted that to specify the pitch shape of a phonological phrase, it is necessary only [to] specify which syllable is accented. [...] Japanese differs from languages with "stress accents" such as English and German in that, at least within the word, there is no such thing as secondary stress in Japanese. sources.quote: The Tokyo dialect of Japanese exhibits lexical contrasts based on pitch accent; that is, there are minimal pairs of words that are identical segment-wise, but can be distinguished in terms of their pitch contours ... Japanese makes lexical contrasts in terms of pitch accent in two ways: (i) presence vs. absence, and (ii) if present, location. ... a. ame+ga (unaccented) 'candy+NOM' b. a'me+ga (accented) 'rain+NOM' ... Phonetically speaking, an accented vowel is assigned a High tone followed by a Low tone on the following vowel, resulting in an abrupt H(igh)-L(ow) fall in F0, whereas unaccented words do not show such a fall. ... for words consisting of n-syllables, there are n+1 accent patterns ... a. i'noti+ga (initial accent) 'life+NOM' b. koko'ro+ga (penultimate accent) 'heart+NOM' c. atama'+ga (final accent) 'head+NOM' d. miyako+ga (unaccented) 'city+NOM' ... Japanese allows only one …

sources.citation: McCawley, James D. (1965). The accentual system of standard Japanese. PhD thesis, MIT, 223 pp.
sources.quote: A sentence of standard Japanese is divided into phonological phrases (bunsetsu) each of which may contain at most one significant fall in pitch. I will refer to the syllable or mora where this fall in pitch occurs as the accented mora or syllable of the phrase. Then, disregarding intonational factors, the morae of a phonological phrase display the following pitches: the morae up to and including the accented mora are high-pitched, except that the first mora is low-pitched if it is not accented; the morae after the accented mora are low-pitched; in phonological phrases which contain no accented mora, the first mora is low-pitched and all subsequent morae high-pitched.
sources.locator: Abstract (p.2) and Chapter III 'Accent', §3.1 General remarks (p.139; scanned text, the text)
sources.note: Classic first-hand generative description: standard Japanese has 'pitch accent' (abstract: 'a phrase can be characterized accentually simply in terms of the location of a fall in pitch and in which there is nothing comparable to the several degrees of stress which can be found in a word in English'); §3.1 adds 'Japanese differs from languages with "stress accents" such as English and German in that, at least within the word, there is no such thing as secondary stress in Japanese'; accent location is lexically free (p.56: possible values 1.n syllables). Confirms the tonal/pitch accent coding.

sources.quote: Both members of each pair had the same accent pattern. [...] The same speaker (naive to the purpose of the experiment) was recorded on digital audio tape producing the cues embedded in the context [CoC'a:], with a high pitch on the [o] and a low one on the [a:]. This accent pattern was chosen because it is common in both the Sino-Japanese and Foreign strata, and because it rules out the possibility of a word boundary inside the stimulus.

sources.note: A speech-perception paper on vowel-length boundaries; subjects are Tokyo-area students. It never describes the accent system, but it treats Japanese word accent as a pitch pattern (H on one mora, L on the next) that varies lexically, which is consistent with the catalog's pitch accent (tonal) coding and with McCawley 1965. Not usable as a primary source for placement.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 6th European Conference on Speech Communication and Technology

sources.citation: Poser, William John (1985). The phonetics and phonology of tone and intonation in Japanese. Massachusetts Inst. of Technology.
sources.quote: In sum, the tone pattern of a Tokyo dialect word is described by two parameters: the presence or absence of an initial low mora, and the presence or absence of a fall from high to low. Moreover, the presence of the initial low mora is predictable. The initial mora is high if the first syllable is heavy or if the following mora is low; otherwise, the initial mora is low. The distinctive property of words is, then, the presence and location of the fall from high to low. [p.29] ... Japanese is not usually described as exhibiting any sort of stress independent of the pitch accent system. There is nonetheless some reason to believe that Tokyo dialect Japanese has a stress system of sorts. [p.42]
sources.locator: Chapter One 'Tone and Accent': §1.2 Tone Patterns, printed p.29 = p.29; §1.3.1 p.35; §1.5 'Stress and Rhythm', printed p.42 = p.42 (MIT text is noisy scanned; wording checked against the tesseract scanned of the same page in the ai.mit.edu copy, /)

sources.citation: Poser, William J. (1984). Phonetics and phonology of tone and intonation in Japanese. Cambridge. Cambridge: Massachusetts Institute of Technology. 374 pp.
sources.quote: Japanese is not usually described as exhibiting any sort of stress independent of the pitch accent system. There is nonetheless some reason to believe that Tokyo dialect Japanese has a stress system of sorts. I have already cited Hattori's report that he has the impression of initial stress on words, and other speakers whom I have consulted confirm this subjective impression. Unfortunately, no instrumental investigation of this point has been carried out. In a similar vein, there is some evidence for phrase-final lengthening in Japanese. This suggests that there may be a word-level pattern of increased duration at the end and "stress" at the beginning.

sources.citation: Poppe, Clemens (2015). Word prosodic structure in Japanese: A cross-dialectal perspective. PhD dissertation, University of Tokyo, 276 pp.
sources.quote: Tokyo Japanese (TJ) is a well-documented variety of Japanese that has played an important role in studies of accent. As can be seen in (1), the nominal accent system is an example of a system with n+1 patterns for nouns with n moras (or syllables). ... [p.21:] According to McCawley (1968), the default accent in Tokyo Japanese is placed on the syllable that contains the third mora from the right (see Chapter 3).
sources.note: Tokyo Japanese has lexical pitch accent with n+1 contrastive patterns (accent on any mora or unaccented); default/antepenultimate accent; the thesis reviews accentual vs tonal analyses (pp.16, 23) but nowhere posits stress. Confirms the tonal/pitch accent coding.

sources.quote: High tones are defined language-dependently. In English, high tones are pitch-accents that contain an H defined in the ToBI prosodic system promoted by Beckman and Ayers Elam (1997). [...] For Japanese, high tonal targets of pitch-accented syllables, which are always high, were chosen. [p.39] ... BI2 and BI3 represent accentual (AP) and intonational phrase (IP) disjunctures, respectively. [p.50]

sources.citation: Kibe, Nobuko (2010). Hogen akusento no tanjo [The formation of various accent systems in Japanese]. NINJAL Project Review 3, 23-35 (in Japanese, English abstract).
sources.quote: すでに多くの研究によって明らかにされているように，東京方言のアクセントは，＜下げ核があるかないか，あるとすればどの拍にあるか＞によって型の種類が区別される体系をもつ。無核の型を含めて，１拍語には２つの型，２拍語には３つの型，３拍語には４つの型，４拍語には５つの型，n 拍語には n＋１の型が存在することになる。 [Translation: As many studies have made clear, the accent of the Tokyo dialect is a system in which pattern types are distinguished by whether there is a fall-kernel (sage-kaku) and, if so, on which mora it lies. Including the kernel-less pattern, 1-mora words have 2 patterns, 2-mora words 3, 3-mora words 4, 4-mora words 5, and n-mora words n+1 patterns.]
sources.note: Primarily about the diachronic origin of dialect accent diversity, but gives a first-hand statement of the Tokyo system: accent = presence/location of a pitch-fall kernel, n+1 patterns. Confirms the tonal/pitch accent coding.

sources.quote: Comparison with the accentual patterns of the simplex words in (4) shows that not only does the accent of the first compound member disappear, but a junctural accent on the first syllable replaces whatever accent the second member has in isolation. ... the Japanese pitch accent is a head feature: Each accent must be the head of some minimal prosodic phrase. This ensures that every minimal [phrase] has at most one accent

sources.quote: Since the size of the underlying domain is not fixed in standard Japanese, the number of types is open, ranging from Type-0 to Type-n in the table. Type-0 is usually regarded as 'unaccented', for the pattern does not have a pitch fall. ... In all other types, the number in the type name signifies the locus of the H tone ... the marked H tone spreads leftward up to the second mora; other moras receive the default L tone.

sources.note: Analyses Tokyo Japanese as a pitch accent (marked-H-tone placement) system with open-ended n+1 patterns; groups it against English stress-accent (Table 1, p.5). Confirms the tonal/pitch accent coding.

sources.citation: Kubozono, Haruo (2006). Where does loanword prosody come from? A case study of Japanese loanword accent. Lingua 116(7), 1140-1170. doi:10.1016/j.lingua.2005.06.010
sources.quote: Most loanwords are known to follow the rule known as 'antepenultimate rule' in (2) if they are lexically accented (McCawley, 1968). ... (2) Loanword accent rule: Put an accent on the syllable containing the antepenultimate mora, or the third mora from the end of the word. ... [p.8:] all three types of words thus described fall into two major accent groups: accented and unaccented. ... Tokyo Japanese further shows a contrast in accent locus for accented nouns. Thus, /í.no.ti/ 'life', /ko.kó.ro/ 'life' and /o.to.kó/ 'man' are accented on the initial, second and final moras, respectively.
sources.locator: accepted MS pp.4-5 (pp.5-6) and p.8 (p.9)
sources.note: Lexical accent (presence and locus) in Tokyo Japanese; antepenultimate default for loanwords (93% accented) vs. majority-unaccented native/Sino-Japanese nouns. Confirms the pitch accent coding and the catalog quote's 'accented on the antepenultimate mora'.

sources.citation: Shimabukuro, Moriyo (2002). A reconstruction of the accentual history of the Japanese and Ryukyuan languages. PhD dissertation, University of Hawaii, 411 pp.
sources.quote: in Tokyo Japanese, which is generally considered to be a prototypical pitch-accent language (McCawley 1978), there are two types of nouns: accented and unaccented. In this dissertation the term 'accent' denotes a distinctive fall or rise in pitch ... [p.12:] Tokyo dialect has locus accent, where pitch fall is distinctive, e.g., atama LHH(L) 'head' vs. kokoro LHL(L) 'heart' (Hirayama 1960) ... [p.318:] Tokyo nouns are distinguished by locus only. ... In Tokyo, the initial syllable is always low pitch unless the syllable is accented.
sources.note: Mainly diachronic/comparative, but §6.2.1 gives a synchronic description of Tokyo accent: locus (pitch-fall) accent, accented vs unaccented nouns, initial-lowering; no stress. Confirms the classification.

sources.citation: Okada, Hideo. 1999 [1991]. Japanese. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, 117-119. Cambridge: CUP (reprint of JIPA 21(2): 94-96, 1991). Rosetta Project copy, archive.org item rosettaproject_jpn_phon-2.
sources.quote: 'There are two lexically relevant pitch levels: high and low. Within a word, if the first mora is high-pitched, the second is inevitably low-pitched, and vice versa. A mora transcribed with an acute accent ... is said to be accented and is high. ... A word with no accent mark begins low and continues high from the second mora onwards. All moras following the accent are low ...' No stress is described; word prosody is presented purely as lexical pitch accent (speech of educated Tokyo speakers).
sources.locator: p.119 (Handbook pagination), section following Conventions; the text
sources.venue: Handbook of the International Phonetic Association

sources.citation: Yoshida, Yuko (1995/1999). On pitch accent phenomena in Standard Japanese. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London.
sources.quote: Theoretically, a lexical accent may land on any one of the vowels in a word. However, in Standard Japanese, if a word consists of three 'syllables (in traditional terms)' or less, the lexical accent location is random, unlike longer words whose accent location is predictable (Haraguchi 1991). Also, it is said that there is class of nouns without lexical accent. [...] Note that the pitch pattern is predictable if the location of the accent is known. [...] accent location in certain classes of words is predictable, and accordingly Standard Japanese should be regarded as any other stress system: to wit, the stress (accent) location is predictable, if it is not specified lexically.
sources.locator: Ch.2 sec. 2.1 'Facts About Pitch Accent and Pitch Pattern in Japanese', printed p.36 (p.37) and p.37 (p.38); last sentence from ch.3 sec. 3.1.2 'The aim', printed p.76 (p.77); file in the nucl1643 mirror folder
sources.note: Government-phonology treatment of Tokyo pitch accent (thesis; Kubozono 2006 lists Yoshida 1999 as a source on accent). No open copy reachable; would corroborate, not change, the classification.

tone.quote: (4) Pitch Accent Principle A pitch accent language has only one pitch, high pitch, which is the immediate interpretation of a pitch accent. ... A (lexical) accent is interpreted as a high pitch, thus an accented vowel is high-pitched. ... In the same manner, in Standard Japanese, the accented nucleus is high-pitched and the other nuclei are simply not high-pitched, that is, pitchless. ... Vowels which are not high-pitched have been said to bear a low tone (Haraguchi 1977, 1991, Poser 1986, Matsumori 1989). There is, however, no evidence for the existence of another tone/pitch. To call what is not H-toned "low-toned" is unwarranted: such vowels are merely pitchless
tone.locator: section 3.2.2 Pitch Accent Principle, pp. 78-79
tone.check: quotation verified in source
tone.summary: Government Phonology account: lexical accent realised as one high pitch on the head nucleus, shared leftwards; 'low tone' rejected as pitchlessness; nouns of up to 3 syllables have n+1 accent classes.

sources.quote: Unlike some other tonal languages, which can have tonal contrasts on all syllables, Japanese allows only one HL pitch fall within a word; this restriction – that there can maximally be one prominence within a word – is sometimes called "culminativity" [...] Given this culminativity restriction, the whole tonal contour of words can be predicted as long as the location of accent (and the presence thereof) is known. sources.quote: A sentence of standard Japanese is divided into phonological phrases (bunsetsu) each of which may contain at most one significant fall in pitch. I will refer to the syllable or mora where this fall in pitch occurs as the accented mora or syllable of the phrase. Then, disregarding intonational factors, the morae of a phonological phrase display the following pitches: the morae up to and including the accented mora are high-pitched, except that the first mora is low-pitched if it is not accented; the morae after the accented mora are low-pitched; in phonological phrases which contain no accented mora, the first mora is low-pitched and all subsequent morae high-pitched. [...] It will be noted that to specify the pitch shape of a phonological phrase, it is necessary only [to] specify which syllable is accented. [...] Japanese differs from languages with "stress accents" such as English and German in that, at least within the word, there is no such thing as secondary stress in Japanese. sources.citation: Labrune, Laurence. 2013. Le japonais. Lalies (Langues et littérature: actes des sessions de linguistique et de littérature) 33: 171-219.
sources.quote: Le japonais de Tokyo est connu pour son accent de hauteur ... Les mots japonais appartiennent à la classe accentuée ou inaccentuée. Les mots accentués possèdent une more qui constitue le noyau accentuel du mot, après laquelle se produit une chute tonale. C'est donc le passage d'une tonalité haute à une tonalité basse qui marque la position de l'accent au niveau du mot. Les mots inaccentués ne possèdent pas de passage de haut à bas. ... a) il n'y a qu'un seul passage de haut à bas dans un mot accentué ... b) les deux mores initiales du mot doivent être de tonalité différente, soit haut - bas, soit bas – haut.

sources.note: Tokyo pitch accent: accented vs unaccented words; accent-nucleus mora followed by an HL fall; surface H/B patterns from two principles; minimal pairs (hashi); accent mainly demarcative/culminative.

tone.translation: Tokyo Japanese is known for its pitch accent ... Japanese words belong to the accented or the unaccented class. Accented words have a mora that constitutes the accent nucleus of the word, after which a tonal fall occurs. It is thus the transition from a high pitch to a low pitch that marks the position of the accent at word level. Unaccented words have no high-to-low transition. ... a) there is only one high-to-low transition in an accented word ... b) the first two morae of the word must differ in pitch, either high-low or low-high.

sources.citation: Katsuda, Hironori. 2025. A probabilistic model of loanword accentuation in Japanese. Phonology 42: e9, 1-26. doi:10.1017/S0952675725100080
sources.quote: Japanese words may be either accented, in which case they carry a single pitch accent (henceforth accent), or unaccented. The presence and location of accents in native and Sino-Japanese nouns have been traditionally considered unpredictable, as exemplified by a well-known triplet: [háɕi] (initial accent) 'chopsticks', [haɕí] (final accent) 'bridge' and [haɕi] (unaccented) 'edge' ... [fn. 1:] In Japanese, accent is phonetically manifested as a steep pitch fall, usually extending from the end of the accented mora to the next mora (Beckman & Pierrehumbert 1986). ... The literature on accent in Japanese loanwords dates back to McCawley (1968), who discovered the 'antepenultimate accent rule'. This rule states that accented loanwords carry an accent on the syllable containing the antepenultimate mora (e.g., [kɯɾisɯ́masɯ] 'Christmas' and [hambáːgaː] 'hamburger'). ... loanwords ending in LH sequences tend to carry an accent on the syllable containing the preantepenultimate mora (e.g., [dókɯtaː] 'doctor' and [béːkaɾiː] 'bakery').

sources.citation: Špica, Dragana. 2024. The Effect of Lexical Accent on Perceived Japanese Vowel Length: Evidence from Croatian. Acta Linguistica Asiatica 14(2): 65-91. doi:10.4312/ala.14.2.65-91
sources.quote: Word accent is free. Every mora in a word has either high (H) or low (L) pitch. Accent is placed on the high mora after which the pitch falls, i.e. H the sequence H⸣L. Accented ones include accent nucleus, i.e. the sequence HL. Once the pitch falls, it does not rise again in the same word. Words in which the pitch does not fall are unaccented or flat. [...] Hence, it follows from the above that patterns *LLH, *HHL, *HLH cannot be found in Japanese (i.e. Tokyo dialect).
sources.locator: p. 68 (section 2.2); bisyllabic and trimoraic pattern inventories p. 69
sources.note: Contrasts the lexical pitch accent patterns of Japanese and Croatian and tests how Japanese pitch patterns (LHL, HLL etc.) in bisyllabic words affect Croatian listeners' perception of vowel length.

sources.citation: Urasoko, Rie. 2023. De-Accentuation in Tokyo Japanese. Radical: A Journal of Phonology, 168-202.
sources.quote: The prominence of a pitch accent is determined by the difference in pitch height. The distinctive lexical pitch accent is marked phonetically by the sequence from high pitched mora (henceforth H) to low pitched mora (henceforth L). This accent is located on the last H pitched mora immediately before the tonal dropping towards L pitched mora, which is called “accent kernel”. Thus, only the tonal fall (HL) marks a placement of lexical accent (if there is one). ... The Japanese lexicon is divided into two accentual patterns: accented and unaccented. ... The accent kernel can be located on any mora.
sources.locator: pp. 169-170, sec. 1.1 'Accent in Tokyo Japanese' (footnote number 1 after 'accent kernel' elided)
sources.note: Tokyo-type pitch accent: words accented (one HL fall, kernel on any mora) or unaccented; H/L are mora pitch heights, no tone count; at least 22 accent-marked forms pp. 170-172.

sources.citation: Golob, Nina. 2022. Word-Prosodic Typology and the Traps of False Similarity: Japanese and Slovene. Acta Linguistica Asiatica 12(2): 115-123. doi:10.4312/ala.12.2.115-123
sources.quote: Tokyo Japanese is known as a typical pitch-accent or non-stress language in the literature as opposed to a stress-accent language like English (McCawley, 1978; Beckman, 1986). [...] It carries a distinctive lexical pitch accent, which is marked phonetically by the tonal change from H to L (Pierrehumbert & Beckman, 1988; Kubozono, 2008). Tokyo Japanese accent/tone is culminative, a property it shares with stress-accent systems. However, the lexicon is divided into tonic words (accented type) with H-L tonal change and atonic words (unaccented type) that convey no such H-L change. In other words, any given word in theory gets n+1 accent possibilities, n being equal to the number of full moras [...] In L1 Japanese, pitch is the only prosodic feature that shows a systemic and uniform response, namely that accented vowels have a statistically higher pitch than the following vowels.

sources.citation: Minamida, Hitomi. 2022. The realization of unaccentedness in Korean and Japanese pitch accent systems. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 9: 1-12. doi:10.3765/amp.v9i0.5192
sources.quote: In lexical pitch accent languages such as Tokyo Japanese, the accentedness or unaccentedness of a word can be detected by looking at the interaction between the word and an enclitic particle. [p. 1] ... the pitch accent melody in Tokyo Japanese is H*+L, which is linked to the accented syllable; +L is realized a bit after the pitch peak H*. In Tokyo Japanese, the accent bearing unit is the syllable, while the tone bearing unit is the mora (McCawley 1968). Only the pitch accent H*+L causes downstep, which is reset at the beginning of each Intermediate Phrase (ip). [p. 2]
sources.note: Compares Daegu Korean final-accented words with Tokyo Japanese unaccented words in phrasal contexts to argue Daegu Korean has an unaccented class.

sources.quote: Tokyo Japanese has only one type of tonal pattern that is lexically relevant, which is realized as a falling pitch contour. Words are either accented or unaccented. Unaccented words are not marked by the lexical falling pitch. Accented words have one 'accented' syllable, which carries the falling pitch contour within itself if it contains a long vowel or a nasal coda, but otherwise exhibits the pitch fall between itself and the following syllable. The pitch shape of individual words is also determined by a variety of intonational features, the most relevant of which for this study is the phrase-initial rise that marks the beginning of an accentual phrase.

sources.quote: Kubozono (2011) argues that the Japanese default accent pattern, which is observed in loanwords and nonce word pronunciation, generally follows the Latin Stress Rule: (i) place the accent on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy (3a), (ii) otherwise place the accent on the antepenultimate syllable (3b). The presence of devoiced vowels does not disrupt this pattern (3c). [...] Japanese strongly disfavors accent on final syllables (Kubozono 2011). [...] In addition, devoiced syllables can bear pitch accents in modern Japanese (Vance, 1987). For example, Japanese accented verbs predictably bear accent on the penultimate syllable; when the penultimate syllables in verbs are devoiced, accent remains on that syllable (e.g. [kaku'su] 'hide'; [tsu'ku] 'to arrive'). Since accent bearing unit in Japanese is a syllable (Kubozono 2011 and many others), this observation too shows that devoiced vowels keep their own syllables.

sources.quote: In Japanese, an accented word is characterized by an initial rise in F0 (unless it bears an initial accent or when its first syllable is heavy CVV or CVN, see Gussenhoven, 2004, pp. 188-189), followed by a sharp fall starting from the accented mora (as shown in the solid curve in Figure 1), which has been transcribed as %L H*+L in the Autosegmental-Metrical (AM) representation (Pierrehumbert & Beckman, 1988). In contrast, an unaccented word has an initial rise (again, unless when its first syllable is heavy CVV or CVN) but no sharp fall [...] (p. 3). [...] we have used a quantitative approach to show that in Japanese the F0 peak associated with a pitch accent varies with its following low tone. We have found evidence that the variable F0 peak height is the result of pre-low raising. Pearson's r reveals an inverse relation between accent peak and the following low tone, and that such relation becomes more pronounced when the peak is further away from the low tone. (p. 24)

sources.quote: The phonetic characteristics of Japanese pitch contours ... include two main features, the initial rise and the accentual fall. The pitch contour of a prosodic word—more precisely, of a minor phrase ...—begins with a boundary %Low and then proceeds on a phrasal High until it reaches the accented syllable, if present. The accentual High*Low complex is a steep fall, as on the syllable ra in a form like tabesaseráreta ‘was made to eat’. In the absence of an accent, as in iresaserareta ‘was made to insert’, the pitch stays on the phrasal High. The concatenation of these tones results in the overall pattern %Low+High+(High*Low)%.
sources.locator: p. 474, sec. 2.1 Preliminaries
sources.note: Tokyo Japanese lexical pitch accent: the accented syllable carries a High*Low fall, docked on its head mora (p. 489, fn. 14); unaccented words stay on phrasal High.

sources.citation: Allen, Blake H. & Masaki Noguchi. 2013. Japanese Accent Shift: Generalizing from Ambiguous Input. LSA Annual Meeting Extended Abstracts (2013): 4 pp. doi:10.3765/exabs.v0i0.782
sources.quote: As shown in (1), verbs in Japanese fall into two prosodic classes: those with accent and those without. Accent on verbs in the accented class typically falls on the penultimate mora or vowel. A small subset of verbs, however, always exhibit accent on the antepenultimate mora, as in (2). By analogy with the shift of accent leftward away from devoiced high vowels (McCawley 1965; Varden 1998), we refer to this antepenultimate accent pattern as accent shift. As (2) illustrates, all accent shift verbs are of the shape ...VV(C)V; they have no consonant between the antepenultimate and penultimate vowels, placing those vowels into hiatus. However, only ten of these "shift-eligible" verbs always exhibit accent shift.

sources.note: Phonological study of Japanese accent shift and how learners generalise the accent pattern from ambiguous input

Indeterminates are divided into two classes: those with initial accent and those without accent. The former have the pitch contour HL...... and the latter LH...... [p. 2] ... sources.quote: It also provides phonetic support for pitch accent in Tokyo Japanese, in the sense that two moras belonging to what is generally considered a heavy syllable can be produced in two different tonal registers. For example, in the trimoraic word kyooto HL 'Kyoto', the pitch fall occurs after the initial mora kyo, and before the second part of the long vowel. [...] First, these elements themselves in principle cannot bear accent. They have the property of causing a leftward shift of the accent when they occupy a prosodic position where an accent would be expected to occur. The traditional approach, represented by Kindaichi & Akinaga (2001), adopts the following rule: accent falls on the antepenultimate mora; if the antepenultimate mora consists of a special mora, accent moves to the preceding mora, falling on the pre-antepenultimate. sources.quote: Word prosody of Tokyo Japanese (simply Japanese hereafter) is often labeled as pitch accent, characterized by a steep F0 fall from the accented mora to the following one (e.g. McCawley 1968). For example, /hana/ with a low-high (LH) tone sequence means 'flower' when the final mora is accented but 'nose' when there is no accent. [...] The results of this study show that, in order for final-accented and unaccented words to be realized differently, they have to be produced with a following particle. Put differently, realizing the contrast is, as it were, all or nothing. When it is realized at all, multiple correlates are observed: F0 rise, F0 peak, and F0 fall. Otherwise the contrast is neutralized, at least in terms of these three measures.

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: In Tokyo, the words in (1) are 'accented' basically on the antepenultimate mora, i.e. a sudden pitch fall occurs between the second and third moras from the end of the word. [...] In Tokyo, so-called 'non-syllabic moras' like the moraic nasal, moraic obstruent and the second half of long vowels and diphthongs, cannot bear an accent. The accent placed on these elements by rule is automatically shifted to the mora immediately preceding them [...] Tokyo Japanese distinguishes between the accent-bearing unit (syllable) and the tone-bearing unit (mora) [...] Particles such as /ga/ and /kara/ do not constitute an independent accentual unit in this dialect, either, but they simply attach to a content word without changing its accent pattern. In other words, the tonal pattern of content words is fixed and does not change in a larger domain [...] Nouns and verbs in Tokyo Japanese can be either accented or unaccented, with the former class of words but not the latter involving an abrupt pitch fall.

sources.citation: Maniwa, Kazumi. 2002. Acoustic and Perceptual Evidence of Complete Neutralization of Word-Final Tonal Specification in Japanese. Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 26: 93-112. doi:10.17161/kwpl.1808.590
sources.quote: Japanese is considered to be a pitch accent language: pitch functions to make lexical distinctions so that the presence or absence of an accent on a particular syllable can predict what word is being uttered. The accent patterns on short phrases in Tokyo Japanese (standard Japanese) are traditionally described as follows: (1) one characteristic pitch pattern, namely a high-low tonal sequence, marks the word accent (2) a word has at most one accent on any mora or can be unaccented [...] Findings suggest that they do not make any distinction in isolated words, but do produce clearly different pitch patterns in a sentence. [...] the present results show that neutralization of the word-final pitch accent distinction in Japanese is phonetically complete for isolated tokens.
sources.note: No abstract; title indicates acoustic and perceptual evidence that word-final accent (tonal) specification is fully neutralized in Japanese.

sources.quote: The privative nature of accent, that is, the presence/absence of accentual marking at some levels plays a crucial role in the linguistic description of accent. ... a tone-sequencing approach by Pierrehumbert & Beckman (1988) gives a linguistically plausible as well as mathematically explicit model of tonal structure in Japanese. ... In PB model, the H* tone belongs to a word level pitch accent while the L% tone belongs to higher level phrases. Due to the fact that the unaccented form has only phrase level tones and no word level pitch accent, it is natural that the categorization between unaccented and accented form always involves phrase level tones.

sources.citation: Kitahara, Mafuyu. 2001. Category structure and function of pitch accent in Tokyo Japanese. PhD dissertation, Indiana University. Ann Arbor: UMI Dissertation Services.
sources.quote: At the level of general description, however, most Japanese linguists and generative phonologists agree on several basic points: (1.1) a. One characteristic pitch pattern, namely a high-low tonal sequence, marks the word accent. b. A word has at most one accent on any mora or can be unaccented. c. Thus, n-mora words have n+1 possible accentuations. ... d. Phrase initial moras have a low tone and second moras have a high tone unless the word in that position has an initial accent. ... At the word level, a pitch accent (H*L) links to a lexically specified mora: [se] in [seetaa] in this case.
sources.locator: pp. 2-3, sec. 1.2.1; last sentence p. 6, sec. 1.2.4
sources.note: Tokyo-type lexical pitch accent: H*L on at most one mora per word, or unaccented (accent-0.n); Pierrehumbert-Beckman framework with phrasal H, L%, catathesis after each H*L; F0 perception tests.

sources.citation: Warner, Natasha. 1997. Recognition of accent patterns across dialects in Japanese. Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 23(1): 364-375. doi:10.3765/bls.v23i1.1283
sources.quote: The dialects of Japanese are divided into three main groups, the Tokyo-type dialects, the Kansai-type dialects, and the accentless dialects. The differences between these three groups are primarily in their pitch accent systems, not in the segmental phonology. [...] For the Tokyo-type dialects, the only aspect of the pitch accent system which is distinctive is the place of pitch fall within a word. Pitch falls after the accented mora, and the first mora of a word is predictably low unless the word has initial accent, so in a word with an accent somewhere other than the first mora, the first mora is low, all moras from the second to the accented one are high, and all moras after the accented one are low. Words with no accent remain high through the last mora. [...] The Kansai-type dialects have this same distinction, but in addition, they distinguish between high-beginning and low-beginning words (examples in 2). The Kansai dialects also have surface final contour tones (rising or falling, abbreviated A for ascending and D for descending) which the Tokyo-type dialects lack.
sources.locator: pp. 365-366 (section II, Background on Japanese dialects)
sources.note: Title indicates a study of pitch accent pattern recognition across Japanese dialects; abstract is only the proceedings header.
sources.venue: Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society

sources.citation: Miner, Kenneth L. 1992. Some Issues in Japanese Accent. Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 17(1): 1-24. doi:10.17161/kwpl.1808.635
sources.quote: Accent is assigned to the nuclei of syllables, but pitch is superficially realized on all moras. A word may be accented on one (and only one) of its syllables, in which case the nucleus of the syllable carries the accent; or a word may be unaccented [...] An unaccented short word-initial mora is low; all subsequent moras from left to right are high until an accented nucleus, if any, is reached, following which there is a fall. [...] I have argued, taking a cue from Pierrehumbert & Beckman 1988, that due to the facts of accent shift, Japanese accent should itself be interpreted as pitch, rather than as a diacritic on the basis of which pitch patterns are imposed by rule. The solution offered here is (a) tentative and (b) concerns only Tokyo Japanese.
sources.note: No abstract; title indicates a discussion of Japanese pitch accent.

sources.citation: Kubozono, Haruo. 1987. The organisation of Japanese prosody. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh. 2 vols.
sources.quote: (12) 1. The primary phonetic feature of the accent is a sudden drop in pitch. 2. The accent-bearing unit, or the unit to which the accent is assigned, is the syllable, and not the mora or any other prosodic unit. 3. There is at most one accent per word or phrase. 4. The location of the accent is unpredictable. 5. Given the location of the accent, however, other pitch features of words and phrases are predictable. ... It is abundantly clear that the Japanese accent is realized as a sudden drop in pitch — this is supported not only by our impressionistic observation but also by a lot of experimental data including my own.

sources.note: Tokyo Japanese pitch accent: lexical accent location per word, realized as a pitch drop; two tone levels H/L favored over H/M/L (pp. 17, 43-46); accent-triggered downstep (catathesis) in vol. 2.

sources.quote: 3.1. For a complete account of the observable pitch variations in Japanese, four phonemically different levels are necessary and sufficient. ... tone.translation: As explained before (this journal no. 49, p. 63), the most rational way to mark accent is to use the three signs (⏋)(—)(⎿) corresponding to the three levels upper, middle, lower. ... As I have said repeatedly, this is a notation of pitch accent and has nothing to do with stress accent. ... ⎿a⏋ozo⏋ra 'blue sky', ⎿ka⏋raka⏋sa 'umbrella', ⎿ko⏋mamono⏋ya 'haberdasher' ... That accent thus appears on several syllables in succession is something researchers have hitherto often hesitated to admit, but ... now that it has been made clear that the accent of Japanese is a pitch accent and that stress accent, even if present, has only secondary significance, such worry is needless.

tone.quote: なお，録音資料のアクセント聞き取りの際には，当然のことながら解釈を加えないで，聞いたとおりに記録した。この資料集で長母音，撥音，2重母音を持つ語でそれらの直後にアクセントの下降を持つ場合が往々出て来るのも，上の態度を貫いたことが一つの理由である。...ただし，促音を含む語においてはアクセントの下降の位置が促音の前にあるか後ろにあるかの判定は困難であり，この場合は一律に促音の前に下降があるものとして処理した。...記録者（または内省者）は，調査語（を含む文節など）が片仮名で示されている記録票に，線を引くなどの方法で，それぞれのアクセントを記入した。それを熟練したアルバイターが数字に変換する作業を行った。
tone.locator: Maegaki §2.4, pp. 7-8
tone.translation: In listening to the accent of the recorded material we naturally added no interpretation and recorded what we heard. That is one reason why, in this collection, words with a long vowel, moraic nasal or diphthong often turn out to have the accent fall immediately after them ... However, in words containing a geminate it is hard to judge whether the accent fall lies before or after the geminate; such cases were uniformly treated as having the fall before it. ... The recorder (or introspecting informant) entered each accent, e.g. by drawing lines, on record sheets showing the survey word (or phrase) in katakana; trained assistants then converted these into numbers.

sources.note: The article argues that the split in Japanese-Ryukyuan tonal correspondences (one Middle Japanese tonal class, Classes 2.3-2.5, matching several Proto-Ryukyuan classes) comes from a conditioned rightward accent shift in pre-Proto-Ryukyuan, blocked by a word-final high vowel or a retained morpheme boundary, so no extra Proto-Japonic tonal classes need reconstructing.
